knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =x^{2} + 1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2 x \\ \text{d}u & =2 x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^{2} + 1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & -1 & 1 \\ u & 2 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{6 x}{\sqrt{(x^{2} + 1)^{3}}}\,\text{d}x=\int_{2}^{2}\frac{3}{\sqrt{u^{3}}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{2}^{2}3u^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u & =- \frac{6}{\sqrt{u}}|_{2}^{2} \\  & =-6\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+6\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3 \sqrt{2}-6\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: a*x^n+b>0 throughout closed original x interval; no poles

knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =3 x^{2} + 4 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6 x \\ \text{d}u & =6 x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=3 x^{2} + 4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 2 \\ u & 4 & 16\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{0}^{2}\frac{12 x}{\sqrt{(3 x^{2} + 4)^{3}}}\,\text{d}x=\int_{4}^{16}\frac{2}{\sqrt{u^{3}}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{4}^{16}2u^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u & =- \frac{4}{\sqrt{u}}|_{4}^{16} \\  & =-4\frac{1}{\sqrt{16}}+4\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}} \\  & =2-4\frac{1}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating a Definite Integral of a Rational Function Using Substitution

question.:question/worked-solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =5 x^{2} - 1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =10 x \\ \text{d}u & =10 x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=5 x^{2} - 1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 1 & 2 \\ u & 4 & 19\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{1}^{2}\frac{10 x}{\sqrt{(5 x^{2} - 1)^{3}}}\,\text{d}x=\int_{4}^{19}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u^{3}}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_{4}^{19}1u^{-3/2}\,\text{d}u & =- \frac{2}{\sqrt{u}}|_{4}^{19} \\  & =-2\frac{1}{\sqrt{19}}+2\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}} \\  & =1-2\frac{1}{\sqrt{19}} \\  & =1 - \frac{2 \sqrt{19}}{19}.\end{aligned}
$$
